Abstract
With the rapid development of high-performance computing ap-
plications, including artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and
scientific simulations, cloud computing platforms are experiencing
unprecedented computational demands. These applications, partic-
ularly resource-intensive tasks such as deep learning model train-
ing, impose stringent requirements on computational resources,
accelerating the widespread deployment of GPUs in data centers.
Traditional CPU-centric architectures struggle to address the esca-
lating demand for parallelism, whereas CPU-GPU heterogeneous
computing environments have become the dominant paradigm in
modern cloud infrastructures due to their exceptional computa-
tional power and flexible resource allocation capabilities. However,
achieving efficient collaborative scheduling of CPUs and GPUs in
heterogeneous cloud environments remains a challenging multi-
constrained, multi-objective optimization problem. Existing sched-
uling algorithms often fail to effectively address critical issues such
as resource heterogeneity, task diversity, and conflicting optimiza-
tion objectives. To tackle these challenges, this paper proposes
an enhanced three-objective collaborative scheduling algorithm
(3OTSO) based on the original Tuna Swarm Optimization (TSO)
framework. The proposed algorithm preserves the global search
capability of TSO while introducing innovative mechanisms to im-
prove multi-objective optimization performance. Comparative ex-
periments and ablation studies conducted on benchmark functions,
together with comprehensive evaluations of the three optimization
objectives and algorithm runtime across diverse cloud computing
environments, collectively validate the robustness and scalability
of 3OTSO.

Introduction
With the rapid advancement of high-performance computing ap-
plications such as artificial intelligence, deep learning, and big data
analytics, cloud computing platforms face escalating demands for
computational power. The widespread deployment of compute-
intensive tasks (e.g., model training, scientific simulations) has
driven large-scale GPU integration in data centers, establishing
CPU-GPU-based heterogeneous computing architectures as a crit-
ical pathway for enhancing system performance and energy effi-
ciency [1–3]. However, the diversity of heterogeneous resources
and task execution dependencies introduce novel challenges in task
scheduling.
Current mainstream scheduling strategies confront threefold
limitations in heterogeneous environments.First, most algorithms
adopt homogeneous assumptions, treating CPUs and GPUs as inde-
pendent resource pools without modeling collaborative execution
across heterogeneous computing units. Second, localized sched-
uling decisions exacerbate resource bottlenecks, making effective
compression of makespan difficult. Third, prevalent issues of low
resource utilization and load imbalance significantly impair system
throughput and Quality of Service (QoS) [4, 14]. Therefore, it is
imperative to develop a multi-objective scheduling mechanism that
synergistically optimizes execution time, resource utilization, and
load balancing.

As a core issue in cloud computing resource management, task
scheduling has been extensively studied. Early heuristic algorithms
like HEFT significantly reduced makespan in heterogeneous envi-
ronments through task priority ranking and processor selection,
establishing itself as a classical benchmark [4]. Subsequent im-
provements such as MPEFT [5] further optimized parallelism and
scheduling length, yet primarily focused on single-objective opti-
mization, struggling to address complex scheduling demands under
multidimensional constraints [6].
To overcome heuristic limitations, meta-heuristic algorithms
have been widely applied in multi-objective scheduling due to
global search capabilities. Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)
achieves rapid convergence through swarm intelligence simula-
tion, demonstrating favorable performance in cloud task schedul-
ing but prone to local optima [7]. Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO),
inspired by wolf pack social hierarchy and hunting behaviors, ex-
hibits strong exploration capabilities yet suffers from parameter
sensitivity and reduced convergence precision in high-dimensional
problems [9].Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) employs spiral
encircling mechanisms but faces premature convergence in high-
dimensional searches [8]. These algorithms still face trade-offs
between convergence speed and solution quality in heterogeneous
environments [15].
Recent research on CPU-GPU collaborative scheduling has pro-
gressed significantly. The HCGTS method dynamically adjusts sub-
task sequences to achieve CPU-GPU load balancing, outperforming
traditional strategies in execution time and energy consumption
[11]. The H-Storm platform customizes FPGA architectures through
heterogeneous task mapping, achieving 3.4× throughput improve-
ment [12]. However, these works primarily target specific appli-
cations with limited generality, seldom simultaneously optimizing
makespan, resource utilization, and load balancing. Additionally,
some machine learning-based scheduling approaches [17] exhibit
high adaptability but suffer from uninterpretable decision processes,
strong training dependencies, and cross-platform reproducibility
challenges [18].
Against the shortcomings, this study adopts the TSO algorithm
[10] as its foundational framework. TSO is an emerging meta-
heuristic algorithm simulating tuna’s spiral foraging and migration
behaviors, featuring fast convergence, strong global search capa-
bilities, and minimal parameters – making it suitable for solving
NP-hard multi-objective scheduling problems. Compared to deep
learning methods, TSO offers superior interpretability and envi-
ronmental robustness, relative to traditional algorithms like PSO,
GWO, and WOA, TSO demonstrates enhanced capacity to escape lo-
cal optima while facilitating multi-objective mechanism expansion.
Building upon TSO, this paper designs a multi-objective scheduling
model tailored for CPU-GPU heterogeneous environments, syn-
ergistically optimizing makespan, resource utilization, and load
balancing metrics. Experimental validation through the CloudSim
simulation platform [13, 16] ensures the proposed method’s effec-
tiveness and stability.
2
Cloud Tasks Scheduling
Figure 1 illustrates task assignment and computational resource
scheduling in cloud computing, using a virtual machine (VM)-based
Figure 1: Task Assignment and Computational Resource
Scheduling in a VM-Based Cloud Environment.
scenario as an example. Cloud task scheduling is structured into
three phases: task launch, execution, and termination. During
the launch phase, the scheduler dynamically allocates CPU/GPU
computing units and associated memory resources (i.e., RAM and
GPU VRAM) based on task profiling and resource demand predic-
tion. In the execution phase, real-time monitoring enables dynamic
adjustment of resource allocations—such as triggering elastic scal-
ing in response to computational deficits or initiating resource
migration under memory pressure. Upon termination, all occupied
resources are promptly released back to the shared resource pool,
enabling immediate reuse.
Physical resource scheduling requires balancing multiple interde-
pendent factors: precise matching of computational requirements
(e.g., CPU/GPU FLOPS), strict adherence to memory constraints
(preventing host memory overflow or GPU VRAM exhaustion), and
dynamic load balancing to avoid node overloading and resource
fragmentation. To establish a systematic scheduling model, this
work conducts a three-tiered analysis encompassing physical re-
sources, scheduling objectives, and algorithm design. In physical
resource modeling, heterogeneous CPU and GPU units are quanti-
tatively characterized in terms of processing power and memory
capacity. For objective modeling, a multi-objective optimization
framework is formulated to simultaneously minimize task comple-
tion time (makespan), maximize resource utilization, and enhance
load balancing—addressing conflicting quality-of-service (QoS) re-
quirements in cloud environments. In algorithm modeling, we
propose 3OTSO, an enhanced metaheuristic algorithm that incor-
porates adaptive weighting and Pareto-optimal set management to
improve global search capability and convergence stability in high-
dimensional, constrained scheduling spaces. This enables effective
trade-off management among competing objectives and enhances
overall scheduling efficiency in CPU-GPU heterogeneous systems.

3
Evaliation
We then compare 3OTSO with the PSO, WOA, GWO, TSO, and ITSO
[19] algorithms. This comparison is specifically structured into two
segments. On the one hand, the convergence performance of the
3OTSO algorithm and its three ablation variants is validated under
standard benchmark functions, on the other hand, experiments are
conducted based on the CloudSim simulation platform to evalu-
ate its performance in terms of key indicators such as total task
makespan, system load balance, and resource utilization. Unlike
the design of the ITSO algorithm, which only targets the scheduling
of CPU-computing tasks, the experiments in this section further
address the collaborative scheduling requirements of dual resources
(CPU and GPU). During the experimental tests, the population size
and number of iterations are set to 50 and 100, respectively. The
experimental environment was configured on a computing system
equipped with an Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 7155U processor (1.70
GHz), 32 GB of main memory, and the Windows 11 operating sys-
tem. All simulation experiments were conducted using CloudSim
(Version 3.0.3) as the underlying simulation framework.

3.2
Evaluation on Cloud Tasks
When conducting simulation experiments on the CloudSim plat-
form, a total of four test schemes were set up. All experiments were
carried out within a single cloud data center, with the scales of tasks
and virtual machines (VMs) gradually scaled up from 5VM-10Task
to 40VM-100Task, as shown in Table 2. Among them, the resource
requirements for a single computing task are set as follows: the CPU
computational demand and GPU computational demand (both in
MIPS) are uniformly distributed within the range of 10000 to 50000,
the memory requirement ranges from 1GB to 4GB, and the GPU
memory requirement is uniformly distributed between 2GB and
8GB. Meanwhile, the weight coefficients 휔₁, 휔₂, and 휔₃ in Equation
10 are set to 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2, respectively. In deadline-constrained
scheduling, where timely task completion is the paramount ob-
jective for deadline adherence, 3OTSO assigns the highest weight
(휔₁ = 0.5) to makespan. To systematically counteract the inherent
resource utilization pressure arising from makespan, load balancing
is allocated a moderate weight (휔₂ = 0.3) to ensure equitable re-
source distribution, while resource utilization is assigned the lowest
weight (휔₃ = 0.2) to prevent load imbalance.
Figure 5 presents a cumulative comparison of the calculation
results of key indicators for multiple algorithms under the above
four scale scenarios, including three indicators, execution time,
system load balance, and resource utilization. To ensure data com-
parability, the statistical results of execution time, load balance, and
resource utilization were all subjected to normalization process-
ing. Additionally, the fitness values calculated by Equation 10 were
negated before finding the maximum value (which is equivalent to
solving for the minimum value of the original multi-objective opti-
mization problem). From the results, it is evident that the 3OTSO
algorithm did not achieve optimal performance in the smallest task
scale scenario (5VM-10Task), where GWO outperformed 3OTSO
by 1.03×. However, 3OTSO achieved the best performance across
the remaining three scale scenarios, exceeding TSO by 1.64× to
9.01× and ITSO by 1.17× to 1.47×, thereby validating its superi-
ority in multi-objective optimization. Furthermore, in the largest
task scale scenario (40VM-100Task), TSO and WOA exhibited the
poorest performance, with 3OTSO outperforming them by 9.01×
and 11.02×, respectively. This aligns with the local optima conver-
gence observed in Figure 3, confirming the robustness of 3OTSO’s
performance across varying problem scales.
Next, we evaluate the scalability of 3OTSO across four distinct
cloud computing scenarios. Table 2 presents the computational
time statistics derived from five independent simulation trials con-
ducted under identical experimental conditions, comparing PSO,
WOA, GWO, TSO, ITSO, and 3OTSO. The minimum value for each
scenario is underlined in Table 2. While 3OTSO achieves multi-
objective collaborative optimization across all scenarios (Figure 5),
its computational complexity yields suboptimal execution times
among the compared algorithms, ITSO demonstrates the highest
computational efficiency. Notably, 3OTSO maintains consistent
execution times, with both average latency and variance falling
within the same order of magnitude as ITSO. Consequently, both the
results in Figure 5 and Table 2 show that 3OTSO retains scalability
even when scaling to larger task sets.
4
Conclusions
This paper addresses the multi-constraint problems in CPU-GPU
resource scheduling within heterogeneous cloud environments
and proposes 3OTSO. By incorporating the Lévy flight strategy,
opposition-based learning mechanism, and dynamic weight ad-
justment framework, the algorithm’s global search capability and
multi-objective balance are enhanced. Dual verification through
theoretical function benchmark tests and cloudsim simulation ex-
periments show 3OTSO can effectively avoid falling into local opti-
mum traps and achieve efficient collaborative optimization in three
aspects, namely task completion time, resource utilization, and load
balancing degree. The algorithm framework proposed in this paper
not only provides a solution that balances efficiency and robustness
for multi-objective scheduling problems in heterogeneous comput-
ing environments but also opens up new technical pathways for
theoretical research and engineering practice in the field of complex
task scheduling.

Abstract: With the rapid development of high-performance computing ap- plications, including artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and scientific simulations, cloud computing platforms are experiencing unprecedented computational demands. These applications, partic- ularly resource-intensive tasks such as deep learning model train- ing, impose stringent requirements on computational resources, accelerating the widespread deployment of GPUs in data centers. Traditional CPU-centric architectures struggle to address the esca- lating demand for parallelism, whereas CPU-GPU heterogeneous computing environments have become the dominant paradigm in modern cloud infrastructures due to their exceptional computa- tional power and flexible resource allocation capabilities. However, achieving efficient collaborative scheduling of CPUs and GPUs in heterogeneous cloud environments remains a challenging multi- constrained, multi-objective optimization problem. Existing sched- uling algorithms often fail to effectively address critical issues such as resource heterogeneity, task diversity, and conflicting optimiza- tion objectives. To tackle these challenges, this paper proposes an enhanced three-objective collaborative scheduling algorithm (3OTSO) based on the original Tuna Swarm Optimization (TSO) framework. The proposed algorithm preserves the global search capability of TSO while introducing innovative mechanisms to im- prove multi-objective optimization performance. Comparative ex- periments and ablation studies conducted on benchmark functions, together with comprehensive evaluations of the three optimization objectives and algorithm runtime across diverse cloud computing environments, collectively validate the robustness and scalability of 3OTSO. ∗Corresponding author.
